report:
## Conclusion

There is **preliminary, moderately encouraging evidence** that acupuncture can reduce depressive symptoms during pregnancy, but the evidence base is limited and not yet definitive.

The strongest single trial is Manber et al.'s 2010 RCT of 150 pregnant women with major depressive disorder, who received either depression-specific acupuncture, non-specific control acupuncture, or massage. Women receiving the depression-specific protocol showed significantly greater symptom reduction and a response rate (≥50% symptom reduction) about 20 percentage points higher than controls, comparable to standard depression treatments of similar duration (journals.lww.com/greenjournal/fulltext/10.1097/aog.0b013e3181cc0816~acupuncture-for-depression-during-pregnancy-a-randomized; med.stanford.edu/news/all-news/2010/02/acupuncture-lessens-depression-symptoms-during-pregnancy-study-shows.html). This was the first RCT specifically testing acupuncture for antenatal depression and remains the most cited evidence.

Subsequent research has built on this but cautiously. A broader meta-analysis of interventions for antenatal depression found "positive results" for body-oriented interventions and acupuncture, though effect sizes were smaller and less robust than for CBT (journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0173397). Later trial protocols, such as the AcuAnteDep study, explicitly describe the evidence as only "preliminary" and call for larger, more rigorous trials before firm conclusions can be drawn (link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-016-1204-9).

**Bottom line:** Acupuncture shows promise as a safe, viable adjunct treatment for antenatal depression, with one solid RCT showing meaningful benefit, but the overall evidence remains preliminary — more large, well-controlled trials are needed before it can be recommended as a proven standalone therapy.
